reconcile.connective: Commentators treat 'sleep' in Psalm 44:23 as figurative for God's seeming inactivity during a delay, not a literal claim clashing with Psalm 121:4's vigilance.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptic's Annotated Bible lists this as a flat contradiction: 121:4's 'neither slumber nor sleep' against 44:23's 'why sleepest thou, O Lord?'

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "Does God sleep?" (skepticsannotatedbible.com/contra/sleep.html)
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (online; contra/sleep.html)

excerpts.excerpt_text: Not that sleep properly falls upon God: the Keeper of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps; his eyes are always upon his people; he never withdraws them from them, and he watches over them night and day: but sometimes he seems and is thought to be asleep; as when wicked men flourish and triumph over the righteous, and go on in sin with impunity; when their judgment seems to linger, and their damnation to slumber, though it does not; and when the saints are under sore afflictions, and the Lord seems to disregard them, and does not appear for their deliverance …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly denies that sleep literally falls on God (matching Ps 121:4's flat denial) while explaining why Ps 44:23's 'why sleepest thou' arises: God only 'seems' asleep when he delays judgment or deliverance.

excerpts.excerpt_text: God is said to sleep when He does not interpose in whatever is taking place in the outward world here below; for the very nature of sleep is a turning in into one's own self from all relationship to the outer world, and a resting of the powers which act outwardly.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: States plainly that 'sleep' is figurative language for God withholding visible intervention, not a literal claim of divine slumber — the harmonizing move against Ps 121:4's flat denial.

excerpts.excerpt_text: This style of addressing God, as indifferent, is frequent (Psa 3:7; Psa 9:19; Psa 13:1, &c.). However low their condition, God is appealed to, on the ground, and for the honor, of His mercy.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Frames the 'sleep' address as a recurring lament convention (citing parallel psalms), not a unique theological claim that God literally sleeps, which is what would clash with Ps 121:4.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874), pp. 57-58
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley catalogs this exact verse pair under 'Does not sleep. / Sometimes' in his Doctrinal Discrepancies chapter (pp. 57-58), arguing that God 'in wisdom, defers the punishment of the wicked, and the deliverance of his people, so that he seems oblivious of both,' so a superficial observer might say 'he sleeps.'
